properties.name: Per-design state never lives in a process-global
properties.statement:
STATE THAT BELONGS TO A DESIGN LIVES ON THE DESIGN HANDLE, NOT IN A `static`. cap:graph-registry names the metadata that must become per-graph rather than per-process; every new process-global that is secretly per-design adds another line to that migration. Legitimately process-wide state is fine and exists today — the seat registry and the serve-shared mode flag are facts about the PROCESS, not about a design. The test is not 'is it a static' but 'would this need a different value for a second design open in the same process'.

ENFORCED — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the enforcement question as it was put to him (gap:ba21fb8550a81e07, "should the build have stopped them, or is that advice?"): "Split it: clause 1 enforced, clause 2 advice."

WHY THIS HALF CAN CARRY ENFORCEMENT AND ITS SIBLING CANNOT — the whole reason the split happened, and it was MEASURED BEFORE THE DECISION RATHER THAN AFTER. A violation of this clause is mechanically visible, because a process-global is a declaration in the source. The codebase holds exactly three runtime process-globals, all in crates/reflow2-core/src/identity.rs: the process's own seat id (`seat_id`, line 357), the attached-seat registry (`ATTACHED_SEATS`, line 486), and the shared-mode flag (`SERVES_MANY_SESSIONS`, line 578). The last two are the ones this rule's own text already calls legitimately process-wide. So enforcement stops nothing today and costs nobody a build; what it stops is the FOURTH one — which is exactly the erosion this rule was written against, one convenient global at a time, invisible until the migration.

WHAT THE CHECK ACTUALLY DETECTS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. ver:no-per-design-process-globals is an allowlist over runtime `static` / `OnceLock` / `OnceCell` / `thread_local!` declarations in the crates' `src` trees. It FAILS when a global appears that the allowlist does not name, so the cost of adding one is stating why it is not per-design. It CANNOT judge whether a struct field is correctly scoped: the per-design metadata that rides on `ReflowService` today (graph_path, write_gen, read_hint) is not a global and the check has nothing to say about it — that is cap:graph-registry's work, and its absence is planned, not a violation. A check that claimed otherwise would be the green-washing the governance skill warns about: attaching a passing check to silence a finding rather than to detect a fault.

THE CLAUSE THAT LEFT: "a design is named by an id that resolves to a location — never a path" is now rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path, and it is ADVISORY. It was split out rather than dropped because the two clauses sit in opposite positions against the code — that one has no compliant surface today, so an honest detector would fail against the entire existing tool surface, and the only ways to make it pass would be to block everything or to attach a check that proves nothing.

EVIDENCE, 2026-08-09, from Anthony's question about running reflow2 behind a web app at 1k / 100k / 1M tenants (dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants). This costs nothing today and is expensive to retrofit, and the failure mode is erosion rather than a decision. reflow2's own design measured 1,828 nodes = 3.8 MB export vs 33 MB store, which is what makes hold-many-designs-per-process the architecture rather than an option.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: nothing about WHERE a design is stored, nothing about hosting, and nothing that requires the registry to be built. It only keeps the door open.
